title: Inside a Training Week at a Spanish Football Academy: What US Coaches Should Expect
excerpt: A day-by-day look at how a Spanish academy structures a training week, and what US coaches can bring home from the rhythm, the drills and the culture.
body:
## The rhythm is the lesson

When US coaches picture a week at a Spanish academy, they often imagine a highlight reel of flashy rondos and famous badges on the training kit. The reality is more useful than that. What actually defines a Spanish academy week is repetition, structure and a shared vocabulary that every coach on the staff uses. Sessions build on each other across the week rather than existing as isolated blocks. If your players arrive expecting a series of one-off clinics, the first thing they will notice is that Monday's work only makes full sense once you have seen Thursday's.

For a visiting US group, the value is in seeing that continuity up close. You are not just collecting new exercises. You are watching how a club sequences a week so that a single idea, say building out from the goalkeeper under pressure, is introduced, isolated, and then stress tested in a game before the weekend. That planning discipline travels home far better than any individual drill.

## A typical weekly shape

Most Spanish youth academies operate on a training week built around a weekend fixture, which shapes everything. A common pattern for an older youth group runs roughly like this: the week opens with lower intensity work focused on possession and organization, ramps up to a high intensity tactical day in the middle, sharpens with speed and finishing later in the week, and finishes with a lighter activation session before the match. Younger age groups train fewer days, often two or three, with a heavier emphasis on technique and small sided games.

The exact split varies by club and age, but the logic is consistent. Load is managed deliberately across the days, hardest in the middle and tapering toward the game. For US coaches used to running a hard session whenever players show up, this intentional undulation of intensity is one of the clearest takeaways. It is not about training harder every day. It is about training the right thing on the right day.

## What a single session looks like

A standard academy session tends to open with a technical or possession based warm up rather than static stretching or laps. Rondos are the classic example, and they are used as a warm up, a teaching tool and a competitive game all at once. From there the session usually moves into a positional or tactical block that mirrors a game situation, then into a larger scrimmage where the day's theme has to appear under real pressure. Coaching happens in short, specific corrections rather than long stoppages.

Sessions are typically 75 to 90 minutes for older groups and shorter for younger ones. The ball is involved almost the entire time. Fitness is rarely trained in isolation for youth players; it is built into games and drills. Visiting coaches often remark on how little standing around there is and how quickly players transition between activities. The tempo of the session itself is treated as a coaching point.

## Day by day, in plain terms

Early in the week the focus is usually recovery and possession. Expect rondos, positional games and technical circuits, with the coaching centered on first touch, body orientation and quick decisions in tight spaces. Midweek is the tactical peak: larger phase of play exercises, work on the specific shape the team will use at the weekend, and defensive organization drilled at match intensity. This is often the most demanding day of the week.

Later in the week the work turns sharper and shorter. Finishing, transitions, set pieces and speed of play dominate, with reduced overall volume so legs are fresh. The final session before a match is deliberately light, often an activation with some ball work, set piece review and a short game. The point is to arrive at the fixture switched on rather than fatigued.

## The culture your players will absorb

Beyond the drills, the biggest difference US groups notice is the coaching culture. Spanish academies obsess over positioning and understanding of the game, sometimes called the tactical dimension, from a young age. Players are expected to know their role in every phase and to make decisions rather than wait for instructions. Coaches ask questions and let players solve problems, and the same terms are used consistently so that everyone reads the game the same way.

There is also a rhythm to the day around the football. Sessions often run in the late afternoon or early evening, after school and after a proper midday meal, which surprises many US visitors used to early practices. The pace of the day, the food, the two footed technical demands and the expectation that players think for themselves all form part of what your players will bring home. That cultural exposure is frequently more memorable to young players than the sessions themselves.

## What US coaches should take home

You do not need a famous crest to copy what works here. The most portable ideas are the ones about structure: plan your week as a sequence, manage intensity across days rather than maxing out every session, keep the ball central, coach in short specific interventions, and use a consistent vocabulary so your players build a shared understanding. Use rondos and positional games as your default warm ups. Let a single theme run through a week so it actually sticks.

If you are bringing a group to Spain, prepare your players before you arrive. Talk to them about tempo, about playing out of pressure, and about being asked to think on the field. Coaches, come ready to observe the planning and the coaching behavior, not just the exercises. Bring a notebook, watch how the staff talk to players, and note how the week fits together. That is where the real return on a training tour lives.
